How AI Is Reshaping Entry-Level Work

By Dana Ortiz, March 2026

Employers adopting generative tools reported that hiring for the most junior roles fell by 13 percent over the past year, according to a survey of large service firms. The decline was sharpest in occupations built around routine drafting, first-pass research, and template-driven code, where a model can produce a serviceable first version in seconds.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Entry-level work has long been the way firms convert codified knowledge into trained judgment: a junior analyst learns by producing the drafts a senior reviews. When a model produces those drafts, the rung of the ladder that turned codified knowledge into experience quietly disappears, and the path from novice to expert loses its first several steps.

Not every occupation moved the same way. In fields where junior tasks require physical presence or accountable sign-off, hiring held steady. Senior workers in the same occupations saw employment hold steady or grow, because their judgment became more valuable precisely as raw drafting grew cheaper. The result is a widening gap between those who can supervise the tools and those who once would have been trained on the tasks the tools now absorb.

What happens next depends on whether firms rebuild the missing training rung deliberately. Some are pairing juniors with models and grading the edits rather than the drafts, on the theory that judgment is still learned by correction. Others are simply hiring fewer people and expecting the survivors to arrive already expert, a bet that pushes the cost of training onto schools and onto the workers themselves.
